final_proof:
Let \(\lambda=\mu+\nu\). We first prove the result when both \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) are finite.

On the real Hilbert space \(L^2(\lambda)\), define
\[
T(f)=\int_X f\,d\nu.
\]
This is well defined and bounded: since \(\nu\leq\lambda\),
\[
|T(f)|\leq \nu(X)^{1/2}\left(\int_X|f|^2\,d\nu\right)^{1/2}
\leq \nu(X)^{1/2}\|f\|_{L^2(\lambda)}.
\]
By the Riesz representation theorem, there is \(h\in L^2(\lambda)\) such that
\[
\int_X f\,d\nu=\int_X fh\,d\lambda \qquad(f\in L^2(\lambda)). \tag{1}
\]
Taking \(f=\mathbf 1_A\), which belongs to \(L^2(\lambda)\) because \(\lambda\) is finite, gives
\[
\nu(A)=\int_Ah\,d\lambda \qquad(A\in\Sigma). \tag{2}
\]
Equation (2) implies \(0\leq h\leq1\) \(\lambda\)-almost everywhere. Indeed, if \(B=\{h<0\}\) had positive \(\lambda\)-measure, then \(\int_Bh\,d\lambda<0\), contrary to (2); and if \(C=\{h>1\}\) had positive \(\lambda\)-measure, then \(\int_Ch\,d\lambda>\lambda(C)\geq\nu(C)\), again contrary to (2). Replacing \(h\) on a \(\lambda\)-null set, assume everywhere that \(0\leq h\leq1\).

Since \(d\lambda=d\mu+d\nu\), (2) yields, for every \(A\in\Sigma\),
\[
\int_A(1-h)\,d\nu=\int_Ah\,d\mu. \tag{3}
\]
Thus the measures \(d\alpha=(1-h)d\nu\) and \(d\beta=h d\mu\) are equal. Also, applying (2) to \(H=\{h=1\}\) gives
\[
\nu(H)=\int_Hh\,d\lambda=\lambda(H)=\mu(H)+\nu(H),
\]
so \(\mu(H)=0\); absolute continuity then gives \(\nu(H)=0\).

Define the measurable function
\[
g(x)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{h(x)}{1-h(x)},&h(x)<1,\\[4pt]
0,&h(x)=1.
\end{cases}
\]
Equality of the measures \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) implies equality of their integrals against every nonnegative measurable function, first for simple functions and then by monotone convergence. Therefore, for every \(A\in\Sigma\), using the nonnegative measurable function \(\mathbf1_{A\cap\{h<1\}}/(1-h)\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nu(A)
&=\nu(A\cap\{h<1\})\\
&=\int_X\frac{\mathbf1_{A\cap\{h<1\}}}{1-h}\,d\alpha\\
&=\int_X\frac{\mathbf1_{A\cap\{h<1\}}}{1-h}\,d\beta
=\int_Ag\,d\mu.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves the finite-measure case.

Now suppose merely that \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) are \(\sigma\)-finite. Choose measurable covers \(X=\bigcup_iP_i=\bigcup_jQ_j\) such that \(\mu(P_i)<\infty\) and \(\nu(Q_j)<\infty\). The countable family \(P_i\cap Q_j\) covers \(X\), and each of its members has finite measure for both \(\mu\) and \(\nu\). Enumerate this family as \((C_n)_{n\geq1}\), and disjointify it by
\[
E_1=C_1,\qquad E_n=C_n\setminus\bigcup_{r<n}C_r \quad(n>1).
\]
Then the \(E_n\) are a measurable partition of \(X\), and both measures are finite on each \(E_n\). For every \(n\), the restricted measure \(\nu|_{E_n}\) is absolutely continuous with respect to \(\mu|_{E_n}\). By the finite case, there is a measurable \(g_n:E_n\to[0,\infty)\) such that
\[
\nu(A\cap E_n)=\int_{A\cap E_n}g_n\,d\mu \qquad(A\in\Sigma).
\]
Define \(g=g_n\) on \(E_n\). This piecewise-defined function is measurable, and countable additivity and monotone convergence give, for every \(A\in\Sigma\),
\[
\nu(A)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\nu(A\cap E_n)
=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\int_{A\cap E_n}g\,d\mu
=\int_Ag\,d\mu.
\]

It remains to prove uniqueness. Suppose \(g_1,g_2:X\to[0,\infty)\) are measurable and induce \(\nu\) in this way. Let \((F_n)\) be a measurable cover of \(X\) with \(\mu(F_n)<\infty\). If \(D=\{g_1>g_2\}\) had positive \(\mu\)-measure, then, because all values of \(g_1,g_2\) are finite,
\[
D=\bigcup_{n,k,m\geq1}
\left(F_n\cap\{g_1\leq k\}\cap\{g_2\leq k\}
\cap\{g_1\geq g_2+1/m\}\right).
\]
Some set \(B\) in this union would have positive \(\mu\)-measure. On \(B\), both functions are bounded and \(\mu(B)<\infty\), so their integrals are finite, while
\[
\int_Bg_1\,d\mu\geq\int_Bg_2\,d\mu+\frac1m\mu(B)>
\int_Bg_2\,d\mu.
\]
This contradicts \(\int_Bg_1\,d\mu=\nu(B)=\int_Bg_2\,d\mu\). Hence \(g_1\leq g_2\) almost everywhere. Interchanging the two functions gives \(g_2\leq g_1\) almost everywhere, and consequently \(g_1=g_2\) \(\mu\)-almost everywhere.
